items.statement:
Assume full AC. Let $G$ be a connected nonempty finite topological graph embedded in a smoothly parametrized two-sphere. Require ordinary supplied line charts along open edges. Every vertex has valence four, with a supplied disk chart in which the four arms are radial, except for auxiliary degree-two subdivision vertices. All four-valent vertices are marked. Vertex-free circle components are allowed. At each four-valent vertex mark the two opposite pairs in its cyclic order.

There is a surface homeomorphism, isotopic to the identity, carrying $G$ to the image of a smooth immersion of finitely many circles whose only multiple points are transverse double points at the marked vertices, with the chosen opposite pairs as the smooth branches. It preserves the cyclic order and any labels on edges and sectors. For a sphere supplied with a smooth product collar in a smooth three-manifold, the surface isotopy extends to an ambient topological isotopy supported in any smaller chosen product neighborhood of that sphere and preserving the sphere. No overcrossing heights or link equivalence are asserted.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every nonempty compact connected boundaryless topological 2-manifold is homeomorphic to the realization of a finite 2-dimensional abstract simplicial complex in which every edge lies in exactly two triangles and each vertex link is a cycle.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For Jordan curves $C$ and $C'$ in $\mathbb R^2$,
every homeomorphism $h:C\to C'$ extends to a homeomorphism
$H:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ that maps the bounded and unbounded complementary
components of $C$ to the corresponding components of $C'$. In particular each
closed bounded Jordan region is a closed $2$-disk.

Assume full AC. Fix a finite cyclic subdivision of $S^1$ into edges. Let $c:S^1\times(0,1]\to S^2$ be continuous, with each $c_r$ an embedding. On every closed edge require that $c$ extends smoothly to an open neighborhood of that edge times each compact positive-radius interval, and has nonzero edge tangent there. At each subdivision vertex require the two one-sided tangent lines of $c_r$ to be distinct for every $r>0$; the family is smooth away from these finitely many corners. Then
$$D=\{0\}\cup\{r c_r(s):s\in S^1,\ 0<r\le1\}$$
forms a standard ball-disk pair: there is a homeomorphism $(B^3,D)\cong(B^3,B^3\cap\{z=0\})$. In particular it is a properly embedded locally flat closed topological disk. There need be no positive lower bound on corner angles as $r\downarrow0$.

More precisely a radius-preserving homeomorphism of $B^3$ carries $D$ to a disk supplied by a smooth positive-radius family of embedded circles. If the subdivision has no corners and the family is already smooth, this preliminary homeomorphism may be the identity.

derivations.claim: Every vertex of the finite graph has even degree, counting a loop twice. Partition its edges into simple cycles by starting with an unused edge, following unused edges until a vertex repeats, removing the resulting cycle, and continuing. At each removal every residual degree remains even, so a nonempty residual component contains another cycle. Splitting a closed walk at repeated vertices gives simple cycles, and each removal decreases the finite edge count. A loop is already a simple circle; insert auxiliary vertices if required for a simple graph presentation. Their embedded images are Jordan circles, have no common edge interiors, and meet only at the finite graph vertices. At an edge point the supplied local line chart has a point off $G$; choose such a point as stereographic pole in the smooth sphere parameter. The graph is then a compact planar drawing. Enclose it in a large round circle $C$ disjoint from it.

Apply the actual construction [F1] to $C$ and these finitely many Jordan circles. Its hypotheses hold even at a cut vertex: intersections are finite points, and no two cycle pieces share an open edge. The exposed-face one- and two-connector stages supply a two-connected root graph containing every cycle before any ear redraw is used. The relative ear induction maps this entire augmentation to a finite polygonal drawing by a plane homeomorphism $\Phi$ equal to the identity outside the disk bounded by $C$. Consequently its subgraph $G$ is polygonal too. This inference retains the actual facial pairing from the ear induction; no uniqueness theorem for abstract planar embeddings is assumed. The homeomorphism is isotopic to the identity relative to $C$: after identifying that round disk with the unit disk use $\Phi_t(x)=t\Phi(x/t)$ for $|x|\le t$, and $\Phi_t(x)=x$ otherwise, with $\Phi_0$ the identity. The boundary formulas agree, the inverse uses $\Phi^{-1}$, and displacement is at most $2t$ at the shrinking center.

Choose disjoint small round disks about the polygonal four-valent vertices, containing only the four initial straight segments and no other graph bend. Their outgoing rays are distinct, since equal rays would share a nontrivial initial segment, contradicting the embedded drawing. In positive cyclic order write their angles as $\theta_0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\theta_3<\theta_0+2\pi$, and let $\psi$ be the increasing piecewise-affine circle homeomorphism taking them to four equally spaced angles $\phi_j=\phi_0+j\pi/2$. Choose increasing degree-one lifts and a smooth radial cutoff $\eta$ equal to one near the center and zero near the disk boundary. The map $(r,\theta)\mapsto(r,(1-\eta(r))\theta+\eta(r)\psi(\theta))$, extended at the center, is a disk homeomorphism: every angular map is increasing, the inverse is continuous, and unchanged radius proves continuity at zero. Its image arms are smooth regular radial graphs, straight near the center and unchanged near the boundary. The marked opposite pairs now join as two perpendicular smooth diameters. Replacing $\eta$ by $t\eta$ gives a boundary-fixed isotopy.

There are finitely many remaining degree-two polygonal bends away from the protected crossing disks. At each choose a disjoint small plane chart containing just its two incident segments. Their outgoing rays are distinct; projection along their difference gives opposite signed transverse components, hence a graph on the two sides of its corner. Apply [F2], with support in that chart and a cutoff equal to one near the bend. The new arc is smooth, equals the old straight segments near the support boundary, and remains embedded. The smooth transition arms from step 3.1 already agree with the old edges on open collars and need no rounding. Thus the resulting drawing is smooth along all open edges, and through each chosen opposite vertex pair, with precisely transverse double points at the marked vertices. Smoothing a vertex-free polygonal circle gives a smooth embedded circle by the same finite construction.

Resolve the marked four-valent vertices according to their opposite pairs in the abstract graph. Every resulting vertex has degree two, so its finite components are circles. The smooth local diameters and the smooth edges from steps 3.1–4.1 give smooth regular parametrizations of these circles, for example by positive arclength; local derivatives are nonzero, and opposite rays form one straight diameter near each crossing. Their image is exactly the regularized graph, and its only coincident image points are the two distinct preimages of each four-valent vertex. Every map used was a surface homeomorphism, so labels and cyclic orders are transported with it. Compose the finitely many isotopies from steps 2.1–4.1, with continuous time reparametrizations at joins, to obtain a surface isotopy $h_t$ from the identity to this regularization.

In a supplied product collar $S^2\times(-\delta,\delta)$ choose a scalar cutoff $\beta(u)$ equal to one near zero and zero near the collar ends. For each $t$ define the ambient map $(s,u)\mapsto(h_{\beta(u)t}(s),u)$ and take the identity outside the collar. This is a homeomorphism: it preserves $u$ and its inverse is $(s,u)\mapsto(h_{\beta(u)t}^{-1}(s),u)$. Joint continuity of both maps follows from the surface isotopy and compactness of its time and surface parameters. It agrees with the identity near the collar boundary and restricts to $h_t$ on the sphere. Choosing a thinner supplied collar gives the requested support. This proves the ambient extension without a smooth isotopy extension assertion for the original topological graph.

boundaries.reason: The graph is nonempty; all vertices are valence four or auxiliary valence two, so an edge exists.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 defines the Alexander isotopy at zero and proves continuity by the shrinking displacement bound; Step 4.1 includes zero marked crossings.
Step 4.1 includes a single vertex-free circle, and Step 3.1 includes one four-valent vertex with loop edges.
Step 3.1 proves distinct outgoing rays by embeddedness; Step 2.1 explicitly handles cut vertices through two-connected augmentation before ear redraw.
Step 3.1 retains the old edges on open disk-boundary collars; Step 6.1 is the identity near both product-collar ends.
The Statement assumes full AC inherited from relative Jordan face extensions in Step 2.1; finite cycles and angular formulas add no choice.

axioms.use: Full AC is inherited from the actual Jordan facial augmentation, relative ear redraw and corner-rounding suppliers. Cycle decomposition, angular interpolation and isotopy extension in a supplied collar are finite explicit constructions.

risk_review.notes: Actual triangulation Proof 4.1–6.1 supplies augmentation and facial pairing; the proof does not infer arbitrary graph redraw from triangulation existence. No overcrossing height or original-link isotopy is claimed.

contract.proof_status_evidence: Six full local proof rows and scoped final checks. Root mathematical acceptance and canonical readiness pending.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
**Given:** A nonempty compact connected boundaryless topological $2$-manifold $M$.

1.1 Assume AC and choose, for every $p\in M$, a disk chart $\theta_p:B(0,2)\to U_p$ with $\theta_p(0)=p$. Put $Q_1=[-1/2,1/2]^2$ and initially $Q_2=[-1,1]^2\subset B(0,2)$. The sets $\theta_p(\operatorname{int}Q_1)$ cover $M$; compactness gives finitely many charts indexed $1,\ldots,n$ whose $Q_1$ interiors still cover. We allow the chart domain disks to be represented by disjoint formal copies; their images in $M$ overlap. The later boundary changes preserve the containment of every original $\theta_i(Q_1)$ in the interior of its new closed chart disk. [A1,L1]

2.1 Replace the initial Q2 by a closed axis-aligned rectangle still contained in D_k and containing Q1 in its interior. Choose its four side levels independently in small allowed intervals near the initial side levels. For each embedded circle, its maximal nondegenerate horizontal or vertical straight subarcs are countable: their relative interiors pull back to pairwise disjoint nonempty open parameter intervals on S¹, and each interval contains a distinct rational parameter after fixing a circular coordinate. Exclude the countably many corresponding horizontal and vertical line levels and the finitely many coordinate levels of old-old crossing points. The four selected sides then contain no old-curve subarc, and no corner or side contains an old-old crossing point. This removes shared C=∂Q2 subarcs; isolated or Cantor contacts are allowed. Choose Q1⊂int Q_n⊂Q_n⊂int Q_w⊂Q_w⊂int Q2, with Q_n and Q_w closed polygonal squares. For an older circle C_j, consider each component I of the parameter preimage of θ_k(int Q2) along its parametrization γ_j:S¹→M. This uses θ_k^{-1} only on actual points in U_k. Call I relevant if its image meets Q_w. Distinct proper components I are disjoint open parameter intervals with endpoints mapping to θ_k(C). Put A=γ_j^{-1}(θ_k(Q_w)) and B=γ_j^{-1}(θ_k(C)), compact disjoint subsets of the parameter circle S¹. Their positive parameter-metric separation is η>0. Every relevant interval contains a point of A and has endpoints in B, so its circular interval length is at least η. There can be only finitely many pairwise disjoint intervals of that length on S¹. This argument uses only the global old-circle parametrization γ_j:S¹→M and compact preimages, not an undefined global chart pullback. An entire S¹ component is one wholly interior Jordan circle, also finite. For a proper I, its closure in S¹ maps injectively to a simple C-to-C arc with distinct endpoints. If its two endpoint images were the same, injectivity forces the endpoints to be the same point of S¹; then I=S¹\{t} and its closure is the *whole* old Jordan circle tangent to C at one point. Include that as a circle piece J, as well as each wholly interior circle. Thus the finite relevant family consists only of distinct-endpoint C-to-C arcs and circle pieces J, with every J contained in cl(int C) and meeting C in at most one point. Pairwise intersections are finite: old-old intersections were finite by the induction invariant; two components of one old circle have disjoint interiors and can meet only at their finitely many listed C endpoints. No relevant piece shares a C subarc by the generic side choice. All nonrelevant components are disjoint from Q_w. Later choose the new polygon Q'' strictly within Φ(int Q_w), around Φ(Q_n); then Φ^{-1}(Q'') cannot meet any nonrelevant component, regardless of infinitely many outer contacts. The wider/narrower separation is essential. [L1,L2,step 1.1]

3.1 Start with polygonal C and all finitely many relevant C-to-C arcs with distinct endpoints. Subdivide at their finitely many mutual intersections and all C contacts, adding degree-two vertices if needed to make a finite simple graph. It is 2-connected. To see this, delete any vertex v. C-v remains connected. Each original C-to-C arc minus v has at most two components, each containing one of its two *distinct* C endpoints unless that endpoint is v; in that case the other component/remaining arc reaches its other C endpoint. Every surviving point of every arc remains attached to C-v. Hence the full graph minus v is connected. Additional subdivisions preserve this property. The outer face is still the exterior of $C$. [L3,F1,step 2.1]

4.1 Let H be the currently included finite 2-connected graph containing C, drawn by arbitrary simple arcs with finite intersections. All its bounded faces are Jordan regions by [F1]. Let K be the finite union of all remaining relevant circle pieces. The full arrangement H∪K is compact, and its finite vertex set V consists of H vertices plus all H-K and K-K crossings/contacts. Assume no shared subarcs, by the generic side choice of step 2.1. If K is nonempty, choose a circle J0 with a free point x in the relative interior of a topological edge of J0\H; if none exists, the remaining circles are already fully represented in H. If J0 meets H in at least two distinct points, it may be added immediately: a cycle meeting a 2-connected graph in two distinct vertices preserves 2-connectivity by the vertex-deletion test. Otherwise J0\H lies in one bounded Jordan face F of H, and choose x in that face away from V. Here “free” is topological; no differentiability of an old Jordan arc is assumed. Choose a relatively open facial-edge subarc $A$ of $\partial F$ disjoint from $K$ and from $V$; finite contact and absence of shared subarcs give one. Choose a compact nondegenerate subarc $A_0\subset A$ and a point $a$ in its relative interior. As $K$ is compact and disjoint from $A_0$, the distance $\delta=\operatorname{dist}(A_0,K)$ is positive. Choose an interior point $z$ of $F$ close enough to $a$ that every nearest point of $z$ on $\partial F$ lies in $A_0$ and $2|z-a|<\delta$; this is possible by taking $z$ on the $F$ side near $a$. Let $y$ be one such nearest point. The open ball $B(z,|z-y|)$ lies in $F$ and misses $K$, since $|z-y|\le|z-a|$ and $\operatorname{dist}(z,K)\ge\delta-|z-a|>|z-a|$. Thus $(z,y]$ reaches $y$ from one component of $F\setminus K$ with no other boundary contact. The point $y$ is **strongly accessible** without any assumed smoothness of the wild edge. The open connected Jordan face $F$ minus the finite set $V$ is polygonally connected, so take a polygonal path in $F\setminus V$ from $z$ to $x$, made transverse to the finitely many polygonal segments already present. Stop it at its first contact $p$ with compact $K$. Because the path misses $V$, $p$ is a free point of a single remaining Jordan circle $J$; its preceding straight segment lies in a component $U$ of $F\setminus K$ and reaches $p$ from $U$. The initial path from $z$ to $p$ can be loop-erased, joined to the straight access segment $y$ to $z$, and shortened at any repeated point to yield a simple polygonal connector $\alpha:y\to p$ whose interior lies in $U$. At both endpoints the connector has a straight final segment. Choose a local Schönflies chart at either free endpoint in which its incident Jordan boundary arc is a diameter; shrink the chart neighbourhood inside a Euclidean ball disjoint from every other finite graph piece, possible because those compact pieces avoid the endpoint. The connector enters the $U$ halfdisk side. These local collars are topological, while the displayed straight segments give the polygonal access actually used; the wild boundary arc need not meet an ordinary Euclidean ball in one connected interval. This finds an exposed $J$ even when other circles are nested behind it. Here $F\setminus V$ is path connected: detour a polygonal path around each of its finitely many removed points inside a small disk in $F$. The first-contact path need not avoid $K$; stopping it finds the exposed circle. [L2,L3,F1,step 3.1]

5.1 Subdivide H and J at their finite common points and at connector endpoints. If |J∩H|≥2, the union H∪J is 2-connected: J with the common points as vertices is a cycle, and deleting any vertex leaves H-v connected plus each surviving J component attached through at least one of two distinct common points. If |J∩H|=1 at v, choose the exposed connector p→y with p≠v on J and y≠v on H. Deleting v leaves J-v joined to H-v by the connector; deleting a vertex of the connector leaves J connected to H at v; all other deletions are immediate. Thus the union is 2-connected. If $|J\cap H|=0$, begin with the simple polygonal connector $\alpha:y\to p$ obtained above, where $y$ and $p$ lie on disjoint Jordan boundary components of the open face $U$. A sufficiently small regular neighborhood of the compact middle part of $\alpha$ is a polygonal ribbon inside $U$, with disjoint left and right long sides. To make this precise, choose disjoint endpoint disks that meet $\alpha$ only in its final straight segments, and let $\alpha_0$ be the closed subarc left after removing their endpoint interiors. The compact set $\alpha_0$ has positive distance from the closed complement of $U$; choose a finite polygonal strip about it thinner than half that distance. Shrink the endpoint disks and strip width together so the two strip ends land on opposite local sides of $\alpha$ in each endpoint disk. At $p$, choose a small Schönflies chart whose halfdisk models the $U$ side of the free Jordan subarc of $J$; choose it to avoid every other finite graph piece. The image of the initial $\alpha$ germ is still a proper embedded arc from the diameter point into that halfdisk. Stop it at its first exit from a smaller closed halfdisk. This is an arbitrary simple crosscut of a Jordan disk. The truncated crosscut has two local sides at each interior point because it is the homeomorphic image of the original straight endpoint segment. The crosscut together with each of the two diameter/boundary subarcs forms a Jordan curve. Apply the arbitrary-simple-arc crosscut proof in `lem-planar-facial-graph-isomorphism-extension` to the halfdisk boundary and this truncated arc: the halfdisk minus it has exactly two open connected Jordan regions, whose frontiers contain the opposite relative open diameter subarcs. Pull these regions back; their frontiers then contain the two free relative open subarcs of $J$ adjacent to $p$, and they are the left and right local $U$ sectors of $\alpha$, even though the Schönflies image of $\alpha$ need not be straight. The same construction at $y$ uses the free facial subarc of $H$. The strip ends just constructed lie in the corresponding local sectors at $p$ and $y$; label those sectors by the two sides of the strip, reversing a local plus/minus name at $y$ if necessary. In each of these four open sectors select a boundary point $q$ in its free $J$ or $H$ subarc away from $\alpha$ and the other finite graph pieces. Pick an interior point $z$ close enough to $q$ that its nearest point on the sector frontier lies in a smaller relative subarc about $q$, which has positive separation from every other local frontier piece. The nearest-ball argument of step 4.1 gives a straight segment from $z$ to a distinct free point $p_+,p_-$ or $y_+,y_-$; its relative interior stays in that sector. Polygonal connectivity of the corresponding sector connects its interior end to the matching long side of the middle ribbon. These four short connecting pieces can be chosen in disjoint endpoint disks and on opposite sides of $\alpha$; erase any self-loops within each side. The result is two disjoint simple polygonal connectors in $U$, $p_+\to y_+$ and $p_-\to y_-$, with four distinct free endpoints. This is the required two-attachment lemma for arbitrary Jordan arcs: the Euclidean ribbon is used only away from wild endpoints, and the endpoint access is supplied by nearest balls in the two local topological sectors. Deleting any vertex leaves one attachment or the other, so $H$ together with $J$ and these two connectors is 2-connected. In all cases subdivide circle arcs and parallel connector arcs as needed to keep the finite abstract graph simple and at least three vertices. Each step adds one previously missing circle piece and uses connectors whose interiors lie in a face of the *full* remaining arrangement, so connectors meet no unprocessed wild circle. The number of remaining circle pieces decreases by one; the process terminates after finitely many steps. Every later circle meets the already included graph only at the originally finite old-old/old-C contacts. The outer C stays a fixed graph cycle and all additions lie inside it. [L2,L3,F1,step 4.1]

6.1 Use the rooted ear decomposition of the final 2-connected finite graph from the fixed cycle C (finite ear lemma Step1.2). Begin with the same polygonal C in the target plane. Maintain an ambient homeomorphism h_i carrying the source partial graph to a polygonal partial graph, fixing C pointwise, and a face bijection induced by h_i. For the next source ear P, its relative interior is disjoint from the partial graph and connected, hence lies in one *bounded* Jordan face F (all additions are inside C). Its distinct endpoints lie on the Jordan frontier of F. The target arc h_i(P) lies in the paired polygonal Jordan face F'. Choose short straight endpoint germs in the corresponding F' sectors, then a simple polygonal path through connected F' joining them and avoiding the existing target graph; mark along it, in order, as many distinct interior points as $P$ has internal graph vertices, and call the resulting polygonal ear $P'$. The Jordan crosscut lemma splits F' along each of h_i(P) and P' into two Jordan disk closures whose boundaries are the corresponding subpath of ∂F' together with the crosscut. Fix ∂F' pointwise and choose a homeomorphism $h_i(P)\to P'$ fixing endpoints and taking each internal ear vertex to its corresponding ordered mark. The resulting prescribed boundary homeomorphism on each pair of split disks extends over that pair by Jordan–Schönflies. The two extensions agree along h_i(P), and both restrict to identity on ∂F'; paste them to a homeomorphism g_i of cl F' and extend g_i by identity outside F'. Then h_{i+1}=g_i∘h_i is an ambient plane homeomorphism fixing C, carrying the new ear to P', and pairing the two new faces by their labelled boundary subpaths. All unchanged faces keep their old pairing. The finite induction produces Φ fixing C and a full β pairing facial cycles and the outer face. It directly supplies the premises of the graph-extension theorem; no unsupported inference from Gallier–Xu Proposition E.3 to β is needed. Gallier–Xu Appendix E Proposition E.3 (PDF p170 / printed p160) supports rooted polygonal ear redraw only. Its Theorem E.2 on the same page explicitly requires facial and outer-face matching. The preceding induction supplies those requirements after finite augmentation. [L2,L3,F1,step 5.1]

7.1 Apply Φ to Q_n,Q_w,Q1 and all older local arcs. The relevant graph is polygonal. Choose a simple polygonal Jordan boundary ∂Q'' between Φ(Q_n) and Φ(∂Q_w), enclosing Φ(Q1), by the following nested polygonal separator lemma; Q'' denotes the closed disk it bounds. For compact nested Jordan disks K⊂int L, apply [F5] with compact K and open U=int L. It supplies a finite polygonal chain Γ with trace in U\K and index n(Γ,x)=1 for every x∈K. Subdivide the finitely many polygonal chain segments at every segment crossing and at every endpoint of a collinear overlap, then combine coincident subsegments and orient negative coefficients backward. The resulting finite directed multigraph is balanced at every vertex because the chain boundary is zero. Starting with any directed edge, follow outgoing edges until a vertex repeats, remove that directed circuit, and continue; balanced degree ensures this exhausts all edges. Split each circuit at repeated vertices. Thus Γ is a finite sum of oriented simple polygonal cycles γ_i. By additivity of index ([F6]), at a fixed x∈K the integers n(γ_i,x) sum to 1, so one is nonzero. Its trace is disjoint from connected K, and index is constant on K by [F6]. The Jordan curve theorem gives a unique bounded complementary region; index vanishes in the unbounded region, so nonzero index places all K in that bounded region. Since γ_i⊂int L and the exterior of the Jordan disk L is unbounded and connected, the closed disk bounded by γ_i lies in int L. This γ_i is the required polygonal separator. Perturb its finitely many vertices by less than half the positive distances of its trace from $K$, from $\partial L$, and between its finitely many nonincident closed edges, and choose the perturbation generically so it crosses polygonal relevant edges only finitely and transversely, away from graph vertices and old-old crossings, with no triple contacts. The straight-line homotopy from the original polygonal cycle to its perturbed version avoids every point of $K$ and stays inside $L$, so winding index at each point of $K$ is unchanged; hence the perturbed Jordan cycle still encloses $K$. Every nonrelevant old component lies outside Φ(Q_w), so Q'' misses it. Set θ'_k=θ_k∘Φ^{-1} on Φ(D_k), and use Q'' as the new closed chart disk. Its image contains the old θ_k(Q1), so the finite interior cover persists. The new boundary is Jordan and meets each earlier boundary in finitely many *topologically transverse* points with no triples. The induction invariant refers only to processed pairs $i<j\le k$; a pair is made finite at its younger index. After $k=n$ all pairs are finite and topologically transverse, with no triple contact. [F1,F5,F6,L2,L3,step 6.1]

8.1 Let Γ=∪_i ∂Θ_i. Make every pairwise crossing a vertex and choose at least three extra vertices on every circle if needed. Between these finitely many marks, the circles give finitely many embedded edges; distinct circles have no shared subarc because all their contacts are isolated transverse points. Γ is a finite graph embedded in M. Every component R of M\Γ has nonempty frontier in Γ: otherwise it would be open and closed in connected M. Every frontier point has a local disk in which Γ consists of one embedded arc or two transverse arcs, so each local sector is adjacent to an open edge side. In particular R touches a side of some edge. A side germ of an open edge belongs to one complement component, and there are finitely many edge sides, hence finitely many R. For each i, R is disjoint from ∂Θ_i. The sets R∩int Θ_i and R\Θ_i are relatively open, disjoint, and cover R, so connectedness puts R entirely inside int Θ_i or entirely outside Θ_i. The interiors cover M, so select i(R) with R⊂int Θ_i(R). This is one choice for each member of a finite set. The closure of R may meet ∂Θ_i(R), which is harmless: the local graph includes that circle as its outer cycle. [L1,L2,step 7.1]

9.1 Fix R and i=i(R). Pull Γ∩Θ_i into the closed plane Jordan chart disk; after a Schönflies boundary homeomorphism it may be viewed inside a closed square C. Each other boundary circle intersects C in finitely many transverse points, with no shared subarc. Its part in the square is a finite union of proper C-to-C arcs with distinct endpoints, or a whole Jordan circle strictly inside C; a circle disjoint from C and outside contributes nothing. Pairwise intersections of these finitely many pieces remain finite. Thus this local graph satisfies the finite arrangement premises of steps 2.1–5.1, with no same-endpoint tangent case needed after transversality. Add C and all C-to-C arcs to get a 2-connected root graph. Process remaining whole circles by the full-arrangement exposed-face construction: 0 common vertices require two disjoint face connectors, 1 requires one, and ≥2 require none. Connector interiors avoid *all* original local curve pieces, including unprocessed circles. The number of circles decreases each step, so the resulting H_i is a finite 2-connected simple plane graph after harmless finite subdivisions. Every added connector lies in a single original component of int Θ_i\Γ, since its relative interior avoids the whole original Γ. By [F1], every bounded face of H_i is a Jordan region whose closed frontier is an embedded graph cycle, and every edge has a face on each side. H_i includes the entire local Γ∩Θ_i. Hence H_i's faces inside the chosen original region R are Jordan regions, and the added connector arcs with relative interior in R partition R into finitely many of them. Retain only those added arcs lying in R, together with their endpoints; discard the additions in other original regions. For different R, repeat independently. Since distinct original regions are disjoint, the retained arc interiors cannot meet across different choices, and all endpoints lie on original Γ or on other retained arcs from that same R. Make the finitely many endpoints common global vertices, choosing distinct free-edge endpoints when possible. The final global Γ' is a finite embedded graph containing Γ. Its complementary regions are exactly the retained local H_i faces, so every region F has a closed Jordan disk closure embedded in M with boundary a simple graph cycle. The two-attachment case is needed here: a single slit of an annulus repeats a boundary shore, while the augmented graph has embedded Jordan facial frontiers. [F1,L2,step 8.1]

10.1 Subdivide every edge of Γ' finitely until it has distinct endpoints and every Jordan facial cycle has at least three distinct edges and three distinct vertices. Edge subdivision does not alter faces or 2-connectivity of the local witness graphs. The vertices, open edge interiors, and open Jordan faces now form a finite regular CW structure on M: each edge closure is an embedded closed interval, each face closure is an embedded closed disk, and distinct open cells are disjoint. Every graph edge has two distinct final adjacent faces. A retained connector lies in one original region $R$ and is an edge of its local $H_i$; the two $H_i$ faces on its sides lie in $R$ and cannot reconnect outside the chart because $R\subset\operatorname{int}\Theta_i$. For an original $\Gamma$ edge, side germs in different original regions remain different; if both lie in one $R$, that edge interior lies in $\operatorname{int}\Theta_i$ and its two local $H_i$ faces in $R$ remain distinct. Thus no bridge or edge bordering the same final face twice remains, and each Jordan facial boundary uses an edge at most once. The local half-plane and transverse-crossing sector charts show each vertex has a single cyclic sequence of incident face corners and edge germs. Fix one homeomorphism $\gamma_e:[0,1]\to\overline e$ for each finite global open graph edge $e$, taking the parameter endpoints to its two graph vertices. For each face F take a convex polygon P_F with one side per boundary-edge occurrence, in cyclic order. Define its boundary homeomorphism to the graph cycle ∂F side by side: on each straight polygon side use the affine side coordinate $t\in[0,1]$ followed by the fixed $\gamma_e$, reversing $t$ when that face traverses $e$ backwards. These maps agree at polygon corners because ∂F is a simple graph cycle, so they assemble into one boundary homeomorphism; extend it over the closed disk by Jordan–Schönflies. Pair corresponding polygon sides by those already fixed boundary parametrizations. Because both copies use the same $\gamma_e$, each paired-side identification is exactly the affine map $t\mapsto t$ or $t\mapsto1-t$ in the side coordinates, despite the wild embedding of $e$ in $M$. The resulting finite polygon quotient maps continuously and bijectively onto M: interiors map to distinct F, open sides to the single corresponding graph edge, and corners to the graph vertices. Compact-to-Hausdorff makes it a homeomorphism. Because each face has at least three distinct boundary vertices, one may triangulate each convex P_F by a fan from an interior point (one triangle per boundary edge). The quotient is a finite regular triangular cellulation; the center is unique to its face and each triangle has three distinct vertices. A boundary edge has exactly two incident triangles, one from each adjacent face; a radial edge within P_F has exactly two incident fan triangles. [F2,L1,L2,step 9.1]

11.1 Let P be the *full* incidence poset of vertex, edge, and triangle cells of that regular triangular cellulation, ordered by inclusion of closures. Include all proper incidences, in particular vertex<triangle even when the intervening edge is omitted from a two-element chain. Let K=Δ(P), whose vertices are cells and whose 2-simplices are strict chains vertex<edge<triangle. Within each closed triangle, these chains are exactly the six barycentric subtriangles. Regularity makes the piecewise affine barycentric maps agree on common subedges and gives a continuous bijection |K|→M; compact-to-Hausdorff makes it a homeomorphism. Every edge of K is one of three types: vertex<edge, edge<triangle, or vertex<triangle. The first lies in exactly two 2-simplices because each original edge has two adjacent triangles. The second lies in exactly two because an original edge has two distinct endpoints. The third lies in exactly two because each original triangle has exactly two edges incident to that vertex. Each vertex link of K is a finite connected 1-manifold: its triangles around a point follow the single cyclic sector order of M, and every link vertex has degree two by the preceding edge count; therefore each link is one cycle. K is finite and 2-dimensional, as required. [F3,L1,step 10.1]

12.1 The complex $K$ of step 11.1 is finite and two-dimensional, its realization is homeomorphic to $M$, each of its edges lies in exactly two triangles, and each vertex link is a cycle. The only unbounded choice is the chart selection in step 1.1; all later selections are finite, while the Jordan and graph suppliers inherit their stated AC hypotheses. This proves the statement. [A1,F1,F2,F3,step 11.1] ∎

## Remarks

The finite arrangement and connector stages work with arbitrary embedded Jordan arcs; no differentiability of chart-boundary curves is assumed. The source Gallier–Xu Appendix E Proposition E.3 supplies the rooted polygonal redraw only after 2-connectivity. Steps 4.1–6.1 prove the missing augmentation and facial pairing.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 At a corner let $a_r,b_r$ be the two unit tangent rays pointing away from that vertex along the incident edges. They depend smoothly on $r>0$ and are linearly independent. In the tangent plane choose the unit $x$ direction parallel to $b_r-a_r$, and the $y$ direction its positive quarter-turn. The two rays have strictly negative and positive $x$ components respectively, since $a_r\cdot(b_r-a_r)=a_r\cdot b_r-1<0$ and $b_r\cdot(b_r-a_r)=1-a_r\cdot b_r>0$. Smooth sphere exponential coordinates in that frame, followed by [F2] on each branch, therefore make the incident curve a graph $y=f_r(x)$, with $f_r(0)=0$, smooth on either side of zero and continuous at zero. The graph chart and its inverse vary smoothly with $r$ on each branch. The corner points, the other parts of the curve and a chosen midpoint of one edge are distinct, so compactness on every closed positive-radius interval permits disjoint corner boxes avoiding that marked midpoint and all other curve pieces. [given, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 Choose positive smooth functions $\rho(r),\kappa(r)$ so that the graph exists for $|x|<\kappa(r)$ and the coordinate box $|x|<\kappa(r),|y|<\rho(r)$ has the separation properties of step 1.1; these two functions may be taken equal to one common valid square-size bound. Here and below these functions are obtained by first taking lower chart-size bounds on each compact interval $[2^{-n-2},2^{-n+1}]\cap(0,1]$, selecting this countable list under full AC, and using a smooth locally finite partition of the radius interval subordinate to their interiors. A weighted average of valid smaller lower bounds is valid, since each active bound is valid at that radius and the conditions persist on shrinking. Such a partition is given by positive bumps divided by their locally finite positive sum. Choose $a(r)<\rho(r)/10$. On $|x|\le\kappa(r)/2$, choose a positive smooth upper bound $M(r)$ for both branch slopes by the same compact-interval method; weighted averages of valid upper bounds remain upper bounds. Set $h(r)=(10/\kappa(r)+100(1+M(r))/a(r))^{-1}$. Then $3h<\kappa/2$ and $|f_r(x)|\le M|x|<a/4$ for $|x|<3h$. Thus the larger box $|x|<3h,|y|<3a$ stays inside the chart, and the finite corner supports remain disjoint and avoid the marked midpoint. Near radius one use a short extension of the given smooth data. All choices have been made on positive radii; no uniform bound at zero is used. [step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Fix a nonnegative smooth kernel $\eta$ supported in $[-1,1]$ with integral one, for example the normalized function $\exp(-1/(1-t^2))$ there. For a positive smooth $\epsilon(r)<h(r)$ define $f_r^\epsilon(x)=\int_{-1}^1 f_r(x-\epsilon(r)t)\eta(t)\,dt$ on $|x|<2h(r)$. If $M(r)$ bounds the two branch slopes, then $|f_r^\epsilon-f_r|\le M(r)\epsilon(r)$. The convolved function is smooth jointly in $r,x$ across zero: rewrite the integral with its smooth translated kernel and split the integration over the two sides of the fixed corner; on a compact radius interval all derivatives on each side are bounded, so differentiation under these finite integrals is valid. Let $\chi$ be smooth, equal to one on $[-1/3,1/3]$ and zero outside $(-1,1)$. Put $g_r=f_r+\chi(x/h(r))(f_r^\epsilon-f_r)$ and $\Delta_r=g_r-f_r$. Then $g_r$ is smooth across zero and equals $f_r$ off $|x|<h(r)$. Choose $\epsilon(r)$ small enough that $|\Delta_r|<a(r)/(10(1+\|\chi'\|_\infty))$; the bounds from step 2.1 allow a positive smooth such choice. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 In this corner box use the fiber map $T_r(x,y)=(x,y+\chi((y-f_r(x))/a(r))\Delta_r(x))$. It sends the graph of $f_r$ to that of $g_r$. Its derivative in $y$ is $1+\chi'((y-f_r(x))/a(r))\Delta_r(x)/a(r)>1/2$. For each fixed $x$ it is therefore an increasing homeomorphism of the vertical interval, equal to the identity near its ends; outside the horizontal support it is the identity too. Thus it is a homeomorphism of the box, and extending by the identity gives a sphere homeomorphism. It depends continuously on $r$, as does its inverse: strict monotonicity with this lower slope bound gives continuous inverses in the vertical coordinate, and the moving chart coordinates are smooth. The nonsmooth $f_r$ in this formula is harmless, since only a homeomorphism is required. Compose over the finitely many disjoint corner boxes. The resulting sphere homeomorphisms $T_r$ and their inverses vary continuously for $r>0$ and carry each original circle to a smooth embedded circle $\Gamma_r$. [step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 These smoothed circles admit a smooth parametrization on $S^1\times(0,1]$. Start at the marked midpoint retained in step 1.1, orient by the original cyclic edge order, and use normalized arclength. In the corner charts the graphs $g_r$ are jointly smooth; outside them the old edges are jointly smooth, and on the overlap the two descriptions agree. Their speeds are positive, so finite chart integration makes their total length and partial lengths smooth on each compact positive-radius interval. Inverting arclength locally by [F2] gives the claimed joint smooth parametrization, and its definitions agree around the whole circle with total length as period. Finally set $T(0)=0$ and $T(r\omega)=r T_r(\omega)$ on the punctured ball. The inverse has the corresponding formula with $T_r^{-1}$. Both are continuous at zero solely because they preserve radius. Hence $T$ is a ball homeomorphism carrying $D$ to the radial surface of this smooth circle family. Apply [F1] to that surface and compose with $T$. This proves the standard pair and local-flatness conclusions, with no corner-angle limit assumed. In the already smooth case take $T_r$ to be the identity and apply [F1] directly. [step 1.1, step 4.1, F1, F2, construct] ∎
